title: What are the disaster-recovery patterns and their RTO/RPO/cost trade-offs (Backup & Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Multi-Site Active/Active), and why must a DR plan be tested, not just documented?
shortTitle: What are the disaster-recovery patterns and their RTO/RPO/cost trade-offs, and why must a DR plan be tested, not just documented?

s1_definition.profdef: Disaster recovery is the set of patterns for restoring a workload in a second location after a regional failure, chosen by two targets: Recovery Time Objective, the maximum acceptable downtime, and Recovery Point Objective, the maximum acceptable data loss. The four classic patterns — Backup and Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, and Multi-Site Active/Active — trade cost for speed: the faster the recovery and the less data you lose, the more you pay to keep the second site ready. A plan must be tested rather than only documented because untested recovery steps silently break and are discovered only during a real outage.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's main branch burns down. Backup and Restore is like keeping the ledgers in a warehouse across town — safe, but it takes a day to rent a new building and move everything in. Pilot Light is keeping a tiny skeleton branch with just the vault running, ready to staff up fast. Warm Standby is a smaller fully-working branch always open on the side, able to take over in minutes. Multi-Site Active/Active is running two equal branches at once, so if one dies customers barely notice. Each option costs more than the last. And a DR plan you have never rehearsed is like a fire drill written on paper but never practised — on the real day, people run to locked doors.
s1_definition.oneliner: RTO is how long you are down, RPO is how much data you lose, the four patterns buy you better numbers for more money, and a plan you never test is a plan that fails when it matters.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Disaster recovery is the set of patterns for restoring a workload in a second location after a regional failure, chosen by two targets: Recovery Time Objective, the maximum acceptable downtime, and Recovery Point Objective, the maximum acceptable data loss. The four classic patterns — Backup and Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, and Multi-Site Active/Active — trade cost for speed: the faster the recovery and the less data you lose, the more you pay to keep the second site ready. A plan must be tested rather than only documented because untested recovery steps silently break and are discovered only during a real outage.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's main branch burns down. Backup and Restore is like keeping the ledgers in a warehouse across town — safe, but it takes a day to rent a new building and move everything in. Pilot Light is keeping a tiny skeleton branch with just the vault running, ready to staff up fast. Warm Standby is a smaller fully-working branch always open on the side, able to take over in minutes. Multi-Site Active/Active is running two equal branches at once, so if one dies customers barely notice. Each option costs more than the last. And a DR plan you have never rehearsed is like a fire drill written on paper but never practised — on the real day, people run to locked doors.

**One line to remember:** RTO is how long you are down, RPO is how much data you lose, the four patterns buy you better numbers for more money, and a plan you never test is a plan that fails when it matters.

sections.s2_technical:
Everything in disaster recovery flows from the two objectives. Recovery Time Objective is the clock: if your RTO is one hour, the business has decided the system can be down for at most one hour before the damage is unacceptable. Recovery Point Objective is the data: if your RPO is five minutes, you can afford to lose at most the last five minutes of data in a disaster. These are business decisions, not technical ones — the technology team's job is to build the cheapest architecture that still meets the numbers the business sets. A core payments ledger might demand an RPO near zero and an RTO of minutes, while a monthly reporting system might happily accept an RTO of a day.

Backup and Restore is the cheapest pattern. You take regular backups and copy them to the recovery region, but you run nothing there until disaster strikes, at which point you provision infrastructure and restore from backup. The cost is tiny — just storage — but the RTO is hours because you build everything from scratch during the incident, and the RPO equals your backup frequency, so hourly backups mean up to an hour of lost data. It suits workloads that can tolerate significant downtime.

Pilot Light keeps the core of the system — typically the database continuously replicating and the machine images ready — running minimally in the recovery region, while the application servers are switched off. When disaster strikes you "turn up the light": start and scale the application tier against the already-current data. The cost is moderate because you pay for a small always-on database replica and storage, the RPO is low because data is continuously replicated, and the RTO is shorter than Backup and Restore because the data is already there and you only need to start the compute.

Warm Standby runs a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the entire system in the recovery region all the time. Everything is live, just smaller, so failover is a matter of redirecting traffic and scaling up. The cost is higher because you run a complete second stack continuously, but the RTO drops to minutes and the RPO is very low. It suits important workloads that need fast recovery without the full expense of running two equal sites.

Multi-Site Active/Active runs full production capacity in two or more regions simultaneously, with live traffic served from all of them. There is no "failover" in the traditional sense — if one region dies, traffic simply shifts to the survivors, often automatically. The cost is the highest because you effectively run the system twice, but the RTO approaches zero and the RPO approaches zero. It is reserved for the most critical workloads where downtime is catastrophic.

The reason a DR plan must be tested, not just documented, is that documentation decays silently. The backup restore script references an old bucket name; the failover depends on a DNS change nobody has permission to make; the replica has secretly been failing for weeks; the runbook assumes a person who left the company. None of these show up on paper — they only surface when you actually execute the plan. A tested DR program runs regular game-days where the team performs the real failover in a controlled window, measures the actual RTO and RPO against the targets, and fixes every gap found. The industry truth is blunt: an untested DR plan is a hypothesis, and you do not want to test your hypothesis for the first time during a real outage with customers and regulators watching.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India three systems need disaster-recovery designs, and the platform team must match each to the cheapest pattern that still meets its business targets — and then prove, through a simulated failover, whether the plan actually hits those targets.

Problem 1 — The core payments ledger cannot lose transactions and cannot be down for more than a few minutes. This is exactly where Multi-Site Active/Active or Warm Standby fits — the business targets are an RTO of minutes and an RPO near zero, so only a pattern that keeps a live second site can qualify. A cheap Backup-and-Restore design would violate both targets.

Problem 2 — The nightly interest-calculation batch can tolerate several hours of downtime and losing up to an hour of recomputable data. This is exactly where Backup and Restore fits — the targets are generous, so paying for a hot standby would be wasted money.

Problem 3 — The customer statements portal should recover within about thirty minutes and lose almost no data. This is exactly where Warm Standby or Pilot Light fits — a small always-on footprint meets the target without the cost of a full active-active deployment.

Problem 4 — A DR plan is documented for the payments ledger claiming a ten-minute RTO, but a game-day simulation reveals the real failover takes forty minutes because of a manual DNS step. This is exactly why testing matters — the documented number was a hypothesis, and only the test exposed that reality breached the target.

The code will model a `DrPattern` with its typical RTO, RPO, and relative cost, a `RecoveryObjective` holding the business targets, a `DrPatternSelector` that picks the cheapest pattern meeting the targets, and a `GameDayValidator` that compares a simulated actual recovery against the target and flags breaches. We will run the three systems plus the failed game-day and print the decisions.

Project structure:

```
disaster-recovery-planner/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/dr/
│   │   │   ├── DrApplication.java                  (main class)
│   │   │   ├── model/
│   │   │   │   ├── DrPattern.java                  (enum with RTO/RPO/cost)
│   │   │   │   └── RecoveryObjective.java
│   │   │   ├── select/
│   │   │   │   └── DrPatternSelector.java
│   │   │   └── validate/
│   │   │       └── GameDayValidator.java
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── dr-targets.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/dr/
│           └── select/
│               └── DrPatternSelectorTest.java
```

Configuration file:

```yaml
# dr-targets.yml — business recovery targets per workload
workloads:
  payments-ledger:
    rto-minutes: 5
    rpo-minutes: 0
  interest-batch:
    rto-minutes: 480     # 8 hours acceptable
    rpo-minutes: 60
  statements-portal:
    rto-minutes: 30
    rpo-minutes: 1
game-day:
  cadence: quarterly     # test the plan, do not just document it
  measure: [actual-rto, actual-rpo]
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the DR planning + game-day demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.dr.DrApplication
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three workloads with their targets — payments-ledger at five-minute RTO and zero RPO, interest-batch at eight-hour RTO and one-hour RPO, statements-portal at thirty-minute RTO and one-minute RPO — plus a game-day on the ledger where the documented ten-minute RTO is tested against an actual forty-minute recovery.

Step 1: The selector receives the payments-ledger objective. It checks each pattern's typical numbers against the targets. Backup-and-Restore fails because its RTO is far too high. Pilot Light fails because its RPO of five minutes exceeds the zero target. Warm Standby fails on the zero RPO too. Only Multi-Site Active/Active, with near-zero RTO and RPO, qualifies, and since it is the only one that meets the targets it is selected despite being the most expensive. The selector logs the choice.

Step 2: The selector receives the interest-batch objective. Here the targets are generous — eight hours and one hour. Backup-and-Restore's typical numbers, roughly eight hours and sixty minutes, fit inside the targets. Because it is also the cheapest pattern, the selector chooses it. Paying for anything hotter would waste money.

Step 3: The selector receives the statements-portal objective of thirty minutes and one minute. Backup-and-Restore fails the RTO, Pilot Light fails the RPO. Warm Standby, at roughly ten minutes and one minute, meets both, and it is cheaper than Active/Active, so it is selected.

Step 4: The validator runs the ledger game-day. The documented target is a ten-minute RTO with zero RPO, but the simulation reports an actual recovery of forty minutes because of a manual DNS change nobody automated. The validator compares forty against ten, finds the RTO breached, and logs a SEVERE game-day failure stating that the documented plan was breached by reality.

Step 5: The final picture shows the lesson clearly. The selection logic matches each workload to the cheapest adequate pattern, but the game-day proves that a number written in a document means nothing until it is executed — the ledger's real recovery was four times slower than claimed, and only the test revealed it.

Final output:

```
INFO: === National Bank of India — DR planning ===
INFO: [payments-ledger] targets RTO<=5m RPO<=0m → choose MULTI_SITE_ACTIVE_ACTIVE (cost rank 4)
INFO: [interest-batch] targets RTO<=480m RPO<=60m → choose BACKUP_AND_RESTORE (cost rank 1)
INFO: [statements-portal] targets RTO<=30m RPO<=1m → choose WARM_STANDBY (cost rank 3)
SEVERE: GAME-DAY FAIL [payments-ledger] actual RTO=40m (target 10m), actual RPO=0m (target 0m) — documented plan breached reality
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Disaster recovery is driven by two business targets. Recovery Time Objective is the maximum downtime the business will accept, and Recovery Point Objective is the maximum data loss it will accept. These are business decisions, and the engineering job is to build the cheapest architecture that still meets whatever numbers the business sets, because recovery speed and data protection both cost money to keep ready.

There are four classic patterns along a cost-versus-speed curve. Backup and Restore is the cheapest — you copy backups to the recovery region but run nothing there, so cost is tiny but recovery takes hours and you lose up to one backup interval of data. Pilot Light keeps the database replicating and images ready while the application tier is off, so cost is moderate, data loss is low, and recovery is faster because you only start the compute. Warm Standby runs a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the whole system all the time, so failover is minutes and data loss is minimal at a higher cost. Multi-Site Active/Active runs full production in two or more regions at once with live traffic everywhere, so recovery time and data loss both approach zero but you effectively pay to run the system twice, which is why it is reserved for the most critical workloads.

The reason a plan must be tested and not just documented is that documentation decays silently. The restore script references an old bucket, the failover needs a DNS change nobody can make, the replica has been quietly failing for weeks, or the runbook assumes a person who has left. None of that shows up on paper — it only appears when you actually execute. So a mature program runs regular game-days where the team performs the real failover in a controlled window, measures the actual recovery time and data loss against the targets, and fixes every gap. An untested DR plan is just a hypothesis, and you never want to test it for the first time during a real outage.

At National Bank of India I did exactly this. I matched our nightly interest batch to cheap Backup and Restore because it could tolerate hours of downtime, the statements portal to Warm Standby for a thirty-minute recovery, and the core payments ledger to an active-active design because it demanded near-zero downtime and zero data loss. Then we ran a game-day on the ledger, and even though the document claimed a ten-minute recovery, the real failover took forty minutes because of a manual DNS step nobody had automated. That single test turned a comforting number on paper into a concrete fix — we automated the DNS cutover — and it is the clearest proof I can give that a DR plan you have never rehearsed is a plan that fails on the day you need it.
